Source blue outlines and red point are ordinary marks rendered black under house style. Coordinates reconstruct proportions without supplying numerical measurements.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use ruler and compasses to apply an enlargement transformation with centre $O$ and enlargement factor $3$. Label your image $A'B'C'$.

answer.short: Triangle $A'B'C'$ with $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$ on rays $OA$, $OB$ and $OC$, respectively, and $OA'=3OA$, $OB'=3OB$, $OC'=3OC$.
answer.worked: Draw rays from $O$ through $A$, $B$ and $C$. Set the compasses to $OA$ and step this distance three times along ray $OA$, starting at $O$, to locate $A'$. Repeat with compass widths $OB$ and $OC$ on the corresponding rays to locate $B'$ and $C'$. Join $A'B'$, $B'C'$ and $C'A'$.

spec.description: Complete enlargement using the same original geometry, with corresponding image coordinates multiplied by three about O. Dashed construction guides distinguish rays from triangle sides.
spec.answerVisibility: Answer-only completed construction.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Verify that each side length of $\triangle A'B'C'$ is three times the matching side length of $\triangle ABC$.

answer.worked:
Measure all three pairs of corresponding sides with a ruler. The measurements should give
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{A'B'}{AB}&=3\\\frac{B'C'}{BC}&=3\\\frac{A'C'}{AC}&=3.\end{aligned}$$
Small differences may arise from construction and measurement accuracy.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use a protractor to verify that each angle of $\triangle A'B'C'$ is equal to the matching angle of $\triangle ABC$.

answer.short: $\angle B'A'C'=\angle BAC$, $\angle A'B'C'=\angle ABC$ and $\angle A'C'B'=\angle ACB$, within measurement accuracy.
answer.worked:
Place the protractor centre at each vertex, align its baseline with one side and measure to the other side. Compare the corresponding measurements:
$$\begin{aligned}\angle B'A'C'&=\angle BAC\\\angle A'B'C'&=\angle ABC\\\angle A'C'B'&=\angle ACB.\end{aligned}$$
Each corresponding pair should agree within measurement accuracy.

children.label: a

spec.description: Complete construction with the original rectangle, four centre-to-vertex segments and the midpoint image.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Join $OA$ and mark the midpoint $A'$ of $OA$.

answer.worked: Draw $OA$ and mark $A'$ on it so that $OA'=A'A=\frac12 OA$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Join $OB$ and mark the midpoint $B'$ of $OB$.

answer.worked: Draw $OB$ and mark $B'$ on it so that $OB'=B'B=\frac12 OB$.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Join $OC$ and mark the midpoint $C'$ of $OC$.

answer.worked: Draw $OC$ and mark $C'$ on it so that $OC'=C'C=\frac12 OC$.

children.label: iv
children.prompt: Join $OD$ and mark the midpoint $D'$ of $OD$.

answer.short: $D'$ is the midpoint of $OD$; the image is rectangle $A'B'C'D'$.
answer.worked: Draw $OD$ and mark $D'$ on it so that $OD'=D'D=\frac12 OD$. Join $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ and $D'$ in order to complete the image.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use compasses to verify that each side length of $A'B'C'D'$ is half the corresponding side length of $ABCD$.

answer.worked:
Set the compasses to each image side in turn. Transferring that span twice along the corresponding original side reaches its other endpoint, confirming
$$\begin{aligned}A'B'&=\tfrac12 AB\\B'C'&=\tfrac12 BC\\C'D'&=\tfrac12 CD\\D'A'&=\tfrac12 DA.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use a protractor to verify that each angle of $A'B'C'D'$ is a right angle, matching the angles of $ABCD$.

answer.short: All four image angles are $90^\circ$, matching the corresponding original angles.
answer.worked: Measure each interior angle of $A'B'C'D'$ with a protractor. Each measures $90^\circ$, within drawing and measurement accuracy. These match the four right angles of rectangle $ABCD$, as enlargement preserves angles.

content.prompt: A ginger cat is sitting on a thin railing 2 metres horizontally from a desk lamp, producing a shadow of the cat on a wall 3 metres behind the cat. What is the enlargement factor of the shadow with respect to the profile of the cat?

answer.worked:
The lamp is the centre of enlargement. The lamp-to-wall distance is $2+3=5\text{ m}$.

$$\begin{align*}k&=\frac{\text{distance from lamp to wall}}{\text{distance from lamp to cat}}\\k&=\frac{5}{2}=2.5\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Ernest is making scale drawings of atoms, in which his drawing of a hydrogen atom is a circle of radius 1 cm. Here are the actual approximate radii of some of the atoms in his drawings, given in picometres
Calculate the radii of Ernest’s drawings of carbon, gold and radium atoms.

answer.short: Carbon: $2.8\text{ cm}$; gold: $5.4\text{ cm}$; radium: $8.6\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
The same enlargement factor applies to every radius. Since $25\text{ pm}$ is represented by $1\text{ cm}$, divide each actual radius in picometres by 25 to obtain its drawing radius in centimetres.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Carbon drawing radius}&=\frac{70}{25}\times1\text{ cm}=2.8\text{ cm}\\\text{Gold drawing radius}&=\frac{135}{25}\times1\text{ cm}=5.4\text{ cm}\\\text{Radium drawing radius}&=\frac{215}{25}\times1\text{ cm}=8.6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: Apply the common length ratio established by the hydrogen drawing to the three other radii; this directly assesses scale drawings.

children.label: i
children.prompt: $\dfrac{PR}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{PQ}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
The matching vertices are $A\leftrightarrow P$, $B\leftrightarrow Q$ and $C\leftrightarrow R$. Ratios of matching sides are equal:
$$\frac{PR}{AC}=\frac{PQ}{AB}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: $\dfrac{QR}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{RP}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
$QR$ matches $BC$, and $RP$ matches $CA$. Hence
$$\frac{QR}{BC}=\frac{RP}{CA}.$$

spec.description: Small triangle DEF beside a larger reflected triangle RST; bases EF and TS are horizontal.
spec.mathematics: D corresponds to R through alpha; E corresponds to S through beta; F corresponds to T.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source vertex and angle labels are visible.

children.label: i
children.prompt: $\dfrac{DE}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{DF}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
The angle labels give $D\leftrightarrow R$, $E\leftrightarrow S$ and $F\leftrightarrow T$. Thus
$$\frac{DE}{RS}=\frac{DF}{RT}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: $\dfrac{FE}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{FD}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
$FE$ matches $TS$, and $FD$ matches $TR$. Hence
$$\frac{FE}{TS}=\frac{FD}{TR}.$$

spec.description: Paired similar quadrilaterals, with the smaller figure rotated relative to the larger.
spec.mathematics: A corresponds to S, B to R, C to U and D to T. Right angles at A, D, S and T; alpha at C and U.
spec.answerVisibility: All original angle cues and vertex labels remain visible.

children.label: i
children.prompt: $\dfrac{AB}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{AD}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
Matching angles and adjacent sides give $A\leftrightarrow S$, $B\leftrightarrow R$, $C\leftrightarrow U$ and $D\leftrightarrow T$. Therefore
$$\frac{AB}{SR}=\frac{AD}{ST}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: $\dfrac{CB}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{CD}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
$CB$ matches $UR$, and $CD$ matches $UT$. Hence
$$\frac{CB}{UR}=\frac{CD}{UT}.$$

spec.description: Two similar open branching figures in different orientations. No closing edges or added angle or parallel marks.
spec.mathematics: L, N, J are collinear; C, B, A are collinear. JK corresponds to AE, MN to DB and JL to AC.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source lines and labels appear.

children.label: i
children.prompt: $\dfrac{JK}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{MN}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
The corresponding long branches are $JK$ and $AE$; the corresponding short branches are $MN$ and $DB$. Thus
$$\frac{JK}{AE}=\frac{MN}{DB}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: $\dfrac{JL}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}=\dfrac{MN}{\boxed{\rule{0pt}{5mm}\hspace{8mm}}}$

answer.worked:
The complete stems $JL$ and $AC$ correspond, as do the short branches $MN$ and $DB$. Therefore
$$\frac{JL}{AC}=\frac{MN}{DB}.$$

children.prompt: A stick 1.5 metres long leans against a wall and reaches 1 metre up the wall. How far up the wall will a ladder 10 metres long reach if it is parallel to the stick?

answer.worked:
Let the ladder reach $h$ metres up the wall. In the diagram, $AB$ is the stick and $CD$ is the ladder.

$\angle AOB=\angle COD=90^\circ$ (wall perpendicular to ground), and $\angle ABO=\angle CDO$ (corresponding angles, $AB\parallel CD$).

Therefore $\triangle AOB\sim\triangle COD$ (AAA).

Matching height and sloping length give
$$\begin{align*}\frac{OC}{OA}&=\frac{CD}{AB}\\\frac{h}{1}&=\frac{10}{1.5}\\h&=\frac{20}{3}=6\tfrac23.\end{align*}$$
The ladder reaches $6\tfrac23$ metres up the wall.

children.prompt: A 3 metre high road-sign casts a shadow 1.4 metres long. How high is a telegraph pole that casts a shadow 3.5 metres long at the same time of day?

answer.worked:
Let $AB$ represent the road-sign and $DE$ the telegraph pole, with shadow ends $C$ and $F$. Let $DE=h$ metres.

$\angle ABC=\angle DEF=90^\circ$ (vertical objects on horizontal ground), and $\angle ACB=\angle DFE$ (the Sun has the same angle of elevation).

Therefore $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF$ (AAA).

Matching height and shadow length give
$$\begin{align*}\frac{DE}{AB}&=\frac{EF}{BC}\\\frac{h}{3}&=\frac{3.5}{1.4}\\h&=3\times\frac{3.5}{1.4}\\h&=7.5.\end{align*}$$
The telegraph pole is $7.5$ metres high.

children.label: c
children.prompt: A steep road rises 1.2 metres for every 6 metres travelled along the road surface. How far will a car have to travel to rise 600 metres?

answer.worked:
Let $AC$ and $DF$ represent distances along the same straight road slope, and let $DF=d$ metres.

$\angle ABC=\angle DEF=90^\circ$ (vertical rise perpendicular to horizontal), and $\angle ACB=\angle DFE$ (the road has the same inclination).

Therefore $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF$ (AAA).

Matching sloping distance and vertical rise give
$$\begin{align*}\frac{DF}{AC}&=\frac{DE}{AB}\\\frac{d}{6}&=\frac{600}{1.2}\\d&=6\times\frac{600}{1.2}\\d&=3000.\end{align*}$$
The car travels $3000$ metres along the road surface.

children.label: d
children.prompt: The front of an A-frame hut is an isosceles triangle of height 5 metres and base 8 metres. How wide will a model of the hut be if its height is 0.8 metres?

answer.worked:
Let $ABC$ be the hut front and $DEF$ its scale model, with perpendicular heights $AG$ and $DH$. Let the model width be $w$ metres.

The model preserves the hut's angles. Thus $\angle ABC=\angle DEF$ and $\angle ACB=\angle DFE$, so $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEF$ (AAA).

The perpendicular heights also form matching right triangles: $\angle AGB=\angle DHE=90^\circ$ and $\angle ABG=\angle DEH$. Hence $\triangle AGB\sim\triangle DHE$ (AAA).

The height of each isosceles triangle bisects its base, so $BG=4$ and $EH=w/2$ metres. Matching sides give
$$\begin{align*}\frac{EH}{BG}&=\frac{DH}{AG}\\\frac{w/2}{4}&=\frac{0.8}{5}\\w&=8\times\frac{0.8}{5}\\w&=1.28.\end{align*}$$
The model is $1.28$ metres wide.

answer.short: $\angle BAP=\angle CAQ$ (common angle) and $\angle APB=\angle AQC=90^\circ$. Therefore $\triangle ABP\sim\triangle ACQ$ (AAA).
answer.worked:
In triangles $ABP$ and $ACQ$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle BAP&=\angle CAQ &&\text{(common angle at }A\text{)}\\\angle APB&=\angle AQC=90^\circ &&\text{(altitudes)}\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ABP\sim\triangle ACQ$ (AAA), with vertices in matching order.

children.prompt: Hence prove that $\dfrac{BP}{CQ}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$.

answer.short: $\dfrac{BP}{CQ}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$, since these are ratios of matching sides of the similar triangles.
answer.worked:
From $\triangle ABP\sim\triangle ACQ$, side $BP$ corresponds to $CQ$, and side $AB$ corresponds to $AC$. Matching sides have equal ratios, so
$$\frac{BP}{CQ}=\frac{AB}{AC}.$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: As an alternative approach, explain why $\dfrac12\times AC\times BP$ and $\dfrac12\times AB\times CQ$ are both equal to the area of $\triangle ABC$.

answer.short: Each is $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{perpendicular height}$ for the same triangle: $AC$ pairs with $BP$, and $AB$ pairs with $CQ$.
answer.worked:
Using base $AC$, the perpendicular height is $BP$, so the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $\tfrac12\times AC\times BP$.

Using base $AB$, the perpendicular height is $CQ$, so the same area is $\tfrac12\times AB\times CQ$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Hence prove that $\dfrac{BP}{CQ}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$.

answer.short: Equating the two area expressions gives $AC\times BP=AB\times CQ$, hence $\dfrac{BP}{CQ}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$.
answer.worked:
The two expressions represent the area of the same triangle:
$$\begin{align*}\frac12\times AC\times BP&=\frac12\times AB\times CQ\\AC\times BP&=AB\times CQ\\\frac{BP}{CQ}&=\frac{AB}{AC}.\end{align*}$$
The final line follows by dividing both sides by $AC\times CQ$.

answer.worked: Write the side lengths as $3s,s$ and $3t,t$, pairing longer sides together. The corresponding side ratios are $3t/(3s)=t/s$ and $t/s$, and all corresponding angles are $90^\circ$. Hence the rectangles are similar.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Any two rectangles whose diagonals meet at $30^\circ$ are similar.

answer.short:
True. The diagonal divides a corner into $15^\circ$ and $75^\circ$ in each rectangle.

The corresponding right triangles are similar by AAA.
answer.worked: A rectangle's diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so the triangles formed by two adjacent vertices and the diagonal intersection are isosceles. The angles at the intersection are $30^\circ$ and $150^\circ$. Their base angles are $(180^\circ-30^\circ)/2=75^\circ$ and $(180^\circ-150^\circ)/2=15^\circ$. Thus a diagonal forms a $15^\circ$–$75^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle in each rectangle. These triangles are similar by AAA, so the rectangles' corresponding sides are proportional. Hence the rectangles are similar.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Any two rectangles whose diagonals have length $6\text{ cm}$ are similar.

answer.short: False. A square of side $3\sqrt2\text{ cm}$ and a rectangle measuring $3\text{ cm}\times3\sqrt3\text{ cm}$ both have diagonals $6\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
For the square, by Pythagoras:
$$\begin{align*}d^2&=(3\sqrt2)^2+(3\sqrt2)^2\\d^2&=36\\d&=6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
For the other rectangle:
$$\begin{align*}d^2&=3^2+(3\sqrt3)^2\\d^2&=36\\d&=6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
Their side ratios are $1:1$ and $\sqrt3:1$, so they are not similar.

children.prompt: Find $AD$, $DC$ and $BC$.

spec.description: Right triangle ADC with altitude DB to horizontal AC; A, B, C occur in order. Ordinary source blue geometry is rendered black.
spec.mathematics: AD perpendicular DC; DB perpendicular AC; AB=9; DB=12; no units supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Only original givens appear.

answer.short:
$AD=15$, $DC=20$, $BC=16$.

Use Pythagoras and proportional sides of the similar right triangles.
answer.worked:
In right triangle $ABD$, by Pythagoras:
$$\begin{align*}AD^2&=9^2+12^2\\AD^2&=225\\AD&=15\end{align*}$$
$\angle ABD=\angle DBC=90^\circ$ and $\angle BAD=\angle BDC$ because both are complementary to $\angle ADB$. Hence $\triangle ABD\sim\triangle DBC$ by AAA.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BC}{DB}&=\frac{DB}{AB}\\\frac{BC}{12}&=\frac{12}{9}\\BC&=16\end{align*}$$
In right triangle $DBC$:
$$\begin{align*}DC^2&=12^2+16^2\\DC^2&=400\\DC&=20\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find $AM$, $BM$ and $DM$.

spec.description: Rectangle BADC, diagonal BD, and perpendicular AM meeting BD at M. All four corner squares and the square at M are retained. Ordinary source blue geometry is rendered black.
spec.mathematics: CD=20; AD=15; AM perpendicular BD; no units supplied.

answer.short:
$AM=12$, $BM=16$, $DM=9$.

Find $BD$ using Pythagoras, then use similar right triangles.
answer.worked:
Opposite sides of the rectangle are equal, so $AB=20$. In right triangle $ABD$:
$$\begin{align*}BD^2&=20^2+15^2\\BD^2&=625\\BD&=25\end{align*}$$
$\angle BAD=\angle BMA=90^\circ$ and $\angle ABD=\angle MBA$ because $M$ lies on $BD$. Hence $\triangle ABD\sim\triangle MBA$ by AAA.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{AM}{AD}&=\frac{AB}{BD}\\\frac{AM}{15}&=\frac{20}{25}\\AM&=12\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{BM}{AB}&=\frac{AB}{BD}\\\frac{BM}{20}&=\frac{20}{25}\\BM&=16\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}DM&=BD-BM\\DM&=25-16\\DM&=9\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: Prove that triangle $ABC$ is similar to triangle $DEC$ and find the value of $e$ and $c$.

spec.description: Opposing triangles share C; A, C, D are collinear and B, C, E are collinear. Matching arrows show AB parallel to DE. Ordinary source-blue geometry is reconstructed in house black.
spec.mathematics: AB=6 cm, BC=4 cm, AC=5 cm, CE=6 cm, CD=e cm, DE=c cm; AB parallel to DE.
spec.answerVisibility: All supplied labels remain visible; no calculated lengths appear.

answer.short:
$\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEC$ (AAA); $e=7\frac12$ and $c=9$.

Use alternate and vertically opposite angles, then the matching-side ratio $6/4$.
answer.worked:
$\angle BAC=\angle CDE$ (alternate angles, $AB\parallel DE$).

$\angle BCA=\angle ECD$ (vertically opposite angles).

Therefore $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle DEC$ (AAA).

Matching sides are proportional:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{CD}{AC}&=\frac{CE}{BC}\\\frac{e}{5}&=\frac{6}{4}\\e&=5\times\frac{6}{4}\\e&=\frac{15}{2}=7\frac12.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{DE}{AB}&=\frac{CE}{BC}\\\frac{c}{6}&=\frac{6}{4}\\c&=6\times\frac{6}{4}\\c&=9.\end{align*}$$
Thus $CD=7\frac12\text{ cm}$ and $DE=9\text{ cm}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that triangle $JNK$ is similar to triangle $JML$ and find the values of $x$ and $y$.

spec.description: Nested right triangles share J and the ray JM. The external double-ended dimension arrow spans JN only. Ordinary geometry is black.
spec.mathematics: J,K,L collinear; J,N,M collinear; KN perpendicular to JL and LM perpendicular to JL; JN=5 cm, KN=3 cm, LM=5 cm, JK=x cm, KL=y cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied dimensions and unknowns only; calculated values are absent.

answer.short:
$\triangle JNK\sim\triangle JML$ (AAA); $x=4$ and $y=2\frac23$.

Use the common angle and right angles, Pythagoras in $JNK$, then proportional sides.
answer.worked:
$\angle NJK=\angle MJL$ (common angle at $J$).

$\angle NKJ=\angle MLJ=90^\circ$ (given).

Therefore $\triangle JNK\sim\triangle JML$ (AAA).

By Pythagoras in $\triangle JNK$:
$$\begin{align*}JK^2&=JN^2-KN^2\\JK^2&=5^2-3^2\\JK^2&=16\\JK&=4\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
Hence $x=4$.

Matching sides are proportional:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{JL}{JK}&=\frac{LM}{NK}\\\frac{JL}{4}&=\frac{5}{3}\\JL&=\frac{20}{3}\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}KL&=JL-JK\\KL&=\frac{20}{3}-4\\KL&=\frac{8}{3}\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
Thus $y=\frac83=2\frac23$.

content.prompt: A vertical stick of length $30\text{ cm}$ casts a shadow of length $5\text{ cm}$ at 12 p.m. Find the length, in centimetres, of the shadow cast by a 1 metre ruler placed in the same position at the same time of the day.

answer.worked:
The stick and ruler form right-angled triangles with their shadows. The Sun has the same angle of elevation, so the triangles are similar (AAA).

The ruler is $100\text{ cm}$ long. Let its shadow length be $x\text{ cm}$. Matching sides give:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{5}&=\frac{100}{30}\\x&=5\times\frac{100}{30}\\x&=\frac{50}{3}\\x&=16\frac{2}{3}.\end{align*}$$
The ruler casts a shadow of $16\frac{2}{3}\text{ cm}$.

content.prompt: You proved in Exercise 9E, Question 8 that the midpoints of the sides of a quadrilateral form the vertices of a parallelogram. Now prove that this parallelogram has area half the area of the original quadrilateral.

answer.short:
The midpoint parallelogram has half the area of the original quadrilateral.

Draw both diagonals. The four corner triangles together have half the quadrilateral’s area, leaving the other half for the parallelogram.
answer.worked:
Let $P,Q,R,S$ be the midpoints of $AB,BC,CD,DA$, respectively. Draw diagonals $AC$ and $BD$. Write $\operatorname{area}(XYZ)$ for the area of triangle $XYZ$.

In triangle $ABC$, $\frac{BP}{BA}=\frac{BQ}{BC}=\frac{1}{2}$ and the included angle at $B$ is common. Thus $\triangle BPQ\sim\triangle BAC$ by SAS. Its base and perpendicular height are each half the corresponding lengths of $\triangle BAC$, so its area is one-quarter as large. Applying the same argument at the other three vertices gives:

$\operatorname{area}(BPQ)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{area}(ABC)$.

$\operatorname{area}(DRS)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{area}(ADC)$.

$\operatorname{area}(APS)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{area}(ABD)$.

$\operatorname{area}(CQR)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{area}(CBD)$.

Let $K$ be the area of $ABCD$. Each diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles, so:

$\operatorname{area}(BPQ)+\operatorname{area}(DRS)=\frac{1}{4}K$.

$\operatorname{area}(APS)+\operatorname{area}(CQR)=\frac{1}{4}K$.

The parallelogram is what remains after removing the four corner triangles. Therefore:

$\operatorname{area}(PQRS)=K-\frac{1}{4}K-\frac{1}{4}K$.

$\operatorname{area}(PQRS)=\frac{1}{2}K$.

Since $PO\parallel AB$, $\angle DPO=\angle DAB$ (corresponding angles) and $\angle PDO=\angle ADB$ (common angle at $D$). Thus $\triangle ADB\sim\triangle PDO$ (AAA), giving
$$\frac{OP}{AB}=\frac{DO}{DB}.$$

$$\frac{BO}{DO}=\frac{AB}{CD}.$$

$$\begin{align*}\frac{BO}{DO}&=\frac{a}{b}\\\frac{BD}{DO}&=\frac{a+b}{b}\\\frac{DO}{BD}&=\frac{b}{a+b}\\\frac{BO}{BD}&=\frac{a}{a+b}.\end{align*}$$

Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal and parallel. Since $K$ and $L$ are midpoints, $AK=DL=CL$ and $AK\parallel DL$. Thus $ADLK$ is a parallelogram because one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel. Hence $KL\parallel AD$, so $\angle AKM=\angle CLM=90^\circ$.

\angle AMK&=\angle CML &&\text{(vertically opposite angles)},\\

\end{aligned}$$

\frac{AX}{XC}&=\frac{AK}{CD}\\
\frac{AX}{XC}&=\frac{AB/2}{AB}\\

answer.short:
The image is an ellipse with fixed endpoints $A'$ and $B'$ and string length $kL$, where $L$ is the original string length and $k>0$ is the enlargement factor.

Every distance is multiplied by $k$, so the constant sum of distances defining the ellipse is preserved in scale.
answer.worked:
Let the string length be $L>AB$, and let $P$ be any pencil position on the ellipse. The taut string gives $AP+PB=L$.

Under an enlargement of factor $k>0$, let $A$, $B$ and $P$ have images $A'$, $B'$ and $P'$. Each interval has its length multiplied by $k$, so
$$\begin{align*}A'P'+P'B'&=kAP+kPB\\A'P'+P'B'&=k(AP+PB)\\A'P'+P'B'&=kL.\end{align*}$$
Also, $A'B'=kAB<kL$. Thus every image point can be reached by a taut string of length $kL$ with fixed endpoints $A'$ and $B'$.

Conversely, applying the inverse enlargement of factor $1/k$ to any point satisfying $A'P'+P'B'=kL$ gives $AP+PB=L$, so it comes from a point on the original ellipse. Therefore the image is exactly the ellipse traced by that new string construction.

answer.worked:
Let the equal altitudes of $\triangle ABC$ be $BP$ and $CQ$, with $P$ on the line $AC$ and $Q$ on the line $AB$.

If $\angle BAC=90^{\circ}$, these altitudes are $BA$ and $CA$, so $BA=CA$ immediately.

Otherwise, consider $\triangle APB$ and $\triangle AQC$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle APB&=\angle AQC=90^{\circ}\\\angle PAB&=\angle QAC\end{align*}$$
The angles at $A$ are both $\angle BAC$, or both its supplement when $\angle BAC$ is obtuse. Therefore $\triangle APB\sim\triangle AQC$ by AAA.

Matching sides give

answer.short:
$BG=2GE$ and $CG=2GF$.

Join $FE$. The midpoint theorem and $\triangle FGE\sim\triangle CGB$ give the ratio $1:2$.
answer.worked:
Join $FE$. Since $E$ and $F$ are the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$, the midpoint theorem gives $FE\parallel BC$ and $BC=2FE$.

In triangles $FGE$ and $CGB$, $\angle FGE=\angle CGB$ (vertically opposite angles) and $\angle GFE=\angle GCB$ (alternate angles, $FE\parallel BC$). Hence $\triangle FGE\sim\triangle CGB$ (AAA).
$$\begin{align*}\frac{CG}{GF}&=\frac{BC}{FE}=2\\\frac{BG}{GE}&=\frac{BC}{FE}=2\\CG&=2GF\\BG&=2GE\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$AD$ passes through $G$.

The same midpoint-and-similarity argument gives the same $2:1$ division point on $CF$.
answer.worked:
Let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$, and let $AD$ meet $CF$ at $G'$. Join $FD$. By the midpoint theorem, $FD\parallel AC$ and $AC=2FD$.

In triangles $AG'C$ and $DG'F$, $\angle AG'C=\angle DG'F$ (vertically opposite angles) and $\angle ACG'=\angle DFG'$ (alternate angles, $AC\parallel FD$). Hence $\triangle AG'C\sim\triangle DG'F$ (AAA).
$$\begin{align*}\frac{CG'}{G'F}&=\frac{AC}{DF}=2\\CG'&=2G'F\end{align*}$$
Part (a) gives $CG=2GF$. There is only one point dividing $CF$ internally in the ratio $2:1$, so $G'=G$. Therefore $AD$ also passes through $G$.

children.prompt: Prove that if two of the medians of a triangle have equal length, then the triangle is isosceles.

answer.short:
If $BE=CF$, then $AB=AC$, so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles.

Use the centroid ratios to obtain $BG=CG$, then prove $\triangle BCF\cong\triangle CBE$ by SAS.
answer.worked:
Suppose the equal medians are $BE$ and $CF$. By part (a),
$$\begin{align*}BG&=\frac23BE\\CG&=\frac23CF\\BG&=CG\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle BGC$ is isosceles, so $\angle BCG=\angle CBG$. Since $C,G,F$ are collinear and $B,G,E$ are collinear, $\angle BCF=\angle CBE$.

In triangles $BCF$ and $CBE$, $BC=CB$ (common side), $CF=BE$ (given) and $\angle BCF=\angle CBE$. Hence $\triangle BCF\cong\triangle CBE$ (SAS), so $BF=CE$.

Since $F$ and $E$ are midpoints,
$$\begin{align*}AB&=2BF\\AC&=2CE\\AB&=AC\end{align*}$$
Therefore $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles. The same argument applies whichever pair of medians is equal.

answer.worked:
In each case, choose $F$ on $RQ$ with $RF=a$. Draw $FG\parallel QP$, meeting $RP$ at $G$, and $FH\parallel RP$, meeting $QP$ at $H$. Quadrilateral $FGPH$ is a parallelogram, so $HP=FG$ and $GP=FH$.

By corresponding angles, $\angle GFR=\angle ABC=\beta$ and $\angle GRF=\angle ACB=\gamma$. Also $FR=BC=a$. Therefore $\triangle GFR\cong\triangle ABC$ by AAS, giving $RG=b$ and $FG=c$.

For $k=2$, $RQ=2a$, so $FQ=a$. By corresponding angles, $\angle HQF=\angle ABC=\beta$ and $\angle HFQ=\angle ACB=\gamma$. Together with $QF=BC=a$, AAS gives $\triangle HQF\cong\triangle ABC$. Hence $FH=b$ and $QH=c$. Using opposite sides of the parallelogram,
$$\begin{align*}RP&=RG+GP\\RP&=b+FH\\RP&=2b,\\PQ&=QH+HP\\PQ&=c+FG\\PQ&=2c.\end{align*}$$
For $k=3$, $RQ=3a$, so $FQ=2a$. The initial AAS proof again gives $RG=b$ and $FG=c$.

The triangles $HQF$ and $ABC$ are equiangular, with $H\leftrightarrow A$, $Q\leftrightarrow B$ and $F\leftrightarrow C$, and $QF=2BC$. Apply the $k=2$ result just proved solely using congruence: $FH=2b$ and $QH=2c$. Therefore,
$$\begin{align*}RP&=RG+GP\\RP&=b+FH\\RP&=3b,\\PQ&=QH+HP\\PQ&=2c+FG\\PQ&=3c.\end{align*}$$

entries.description:
This chapter introduces a transformation called an enlargement. This allows us to develop the idea of similar figures, which is a more general idea than congruence.

For example, the two right-angled triangles shown here are similar because they have exactly the same shape, but they are not congruent because they have different side lengths.

Similarity and proportion are closely related, as we shall see. This idea has been used in art and architecture for centuries. It is now used extensively in photography and in the zoom function of a computer application.
